analysis.one_liner: Requires makers of cribs, strollers, and other baby gear to include registration cards so families learn about recalls.
analysis.headline: The House passed it by voice vote on October 9, 2007; the Senate committee never acted, and the bill died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill tells the Consumer Product Safety Commission to make manufacturers of durable baby and toddler products — cribs, strollers, high chairs, carriers, swings and more — include a postage-paid registration card with every product, keep a record of who registers, and permanently label each product with the maker's name, model number, and manufacture date. The point is simple: when a product is recalled, the maker can contact the families who own it instead of waiting for them to hear about it in the news. Parents with registered products would get direct notice of recalls and safety alerts; the information could be used for nothing else.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with young children. The bill's own findings note an average of 50 children under 5 die each year in incidents involving nursery products, and children's products made up 27% of the roughly 400 recalls in fiscal 2005 — nearly 20 million recalled units. Registration means a family can be contacted directly when the crib or stroller they bought turns out to be dangerous, instead of relying on news reports they may never see.

how_it_helps.text: Requires a postage-paid registration form attached to each durable infant or toddler product, with an option to register online, so ownership can be traced to the buyer.
Requires manufacturers to keep registrants' contact information for at least six years and use it to notify families during a recall or safety alert.
Requires permanent labeling with the manufacturer, model name and number, and date of manufacture, making it possible to identify whether a specific product is covered by a recall.
Bars manufacturers from using or sharing registration information for any purpose other than recall and safety notifications, addressing the privacy concern the data collection raises.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of durable infant and toddler products — crib, stroller, high chair, carrier, and similar makers — bear the cost of printing and attaching registration forms, running online registration, maintaining six years of consumer records, and permanent product labeling. Some of that cost would likely show up in prices; most of these products already cost relatively little, and the compliance burden is administrative rather than a redesign requirement.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes new paperwork and recordkeeping obligations — registration forms with every unit, six-year consumer contact records, and permanent labeling — on manufacturers, costs that could be passed to consumers in prices.

The approach depends on families actually filling out and returning the card, which historically only a fraction do; the bill itself orders the CPSC to study and report to Congress on how effective the forms actually are at facilitating recalls, an implicit acknowledgment that the mechanism is unproven.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and targeted: parents learn directly when the crib, stroller, or carrier their baby sleeps in has been recalled, and children's products were being recalled roughly twice a week. The costs are real but modest — administrative compliance for manufacturers, no mandated redesign, and a privacy restriction limiting the data to recall use. An honest supporter would admit the registration-card mechanism works only as well as families' willingness to return the cards, which is why the bill built in a CPSC effectiveness study. On balance, a low-cost measure aimed at reducing injuries and deaths among children under 5.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it without opposition by voice vote, but the Senate Commerce Committee never took it up, and it expired when that Congress ended in January 2009. (The same registration-card requirements were subsequently enacted later in 2008 as part of the broader Consumer Product Safety Improvement Act, which did become law.)

narrative.text: Introduced in March 2007 with bipartisan sponsorship, the bill moved through the House Energy and Commerce Committee — subcommittee hearings in June, subcommittee mark-up in July, full committee mark-up in September — and was reported amended in October 2007.
On October 9, 2007, the House passed the bill by voice vote under suspension of the rules, a fast-track procedure reserved for noncontroversial measures.

Six days later the Senate received the bill and referred it to its Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee, where it sat with no further action through the end of the Congress on January 3, 2009.

The registration-card and labeling requirements the bill envisioned were enacted months later, in 2008, as part of the Consumer Product Safety Improvement Act, a broader product-safety law named in part for Danny Keysar.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: In the short term, manufacturers of cribs, strollers, and similar products avoided the registration and recordkeeping requirements, but only briefly — the same requirements were enacted in the broader 2008 consumer product safety law. The bill's failure as a standalone measure cost families relatively little in the end, though it delayed direct recall notification.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Baby product makers, briefly, until a 2008 law enacted it

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, named for Danny Keysar, a Chicago toddler killed by a recalled crib, and steered it through House committee.

for.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
for.what_they_did: Held subcommittee and full committee mark-ups and reported the bill amended in October 2007.

for.name: The House of Representatives
for.what_they_did: Passed the bill by voice vote on October 9, 2007, with no recorded opposition.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on October 15, 2007 and never reported it or scheduled any action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had 11 cosponsors (10 Democrats, 1 Republican) and passed the House by voice vote with no recorded opposition; its death in the Senate committee was quiet rather than partisan. [S5][S6]

industries.industry: Manufacturers of durable infant and toddler products (cribs, strollers, high chairs, carriers, swings)
industries.note: The bill requires a postage-paid registration card with every unit, six years of consumer contact records, permanent product labeling, and a ban on using registration data for marketing — administrative costs that fall entirely on these manufacturers. Their interest in defeating or delaying the bill ran against families' interest in being told directly about recalls of the products their children use.

The bill hands the CPSC new mandatory rulemaking duties plus an effectiveness study, expanding its workload but also its role in protecting children. Consumer-safety regulators and the families they serve pull in the same direction here.
